unit.why: An anecdote about the Shakh, a 17th-century rabbinic authority outside Hasidism: his in-laws test his luck in trade, and he declines to trade again.

stories.start_quote: שמעתי מעשה כשהי׳ הש"ך ז"ל אכל מזונות
stories.summary_en: The Shakh, supported by his wealthy father-in-law, is sent to the market and succeeds, but the second time he refuses, reading 'the enemy said I will pursue' as Satan's ploy to make him forget his learning through profit and then take the money too.

tags.why: Praises the piety of a pre-Hasidic rabbinic authority

quotes: ובשעת הלמוד היה נותן לו חותנו
עד שיסחור כ״כ זמן מרובה שישכח תלמודו
tags.why: Devotion to Torah study is the central value
His in-laws are the ones who send him to trade
His mother-in-law joins in urging him

quotes: אמר אויב זה השטן ארדוף אותו
tags.why: Exegesis of a verse justifies his decision

quotes: ושמחו מאד שראו איך שיש לו
tags.why: The in-laws rejoice at his success
Shows that Torah comes before worldly profit

missing_concepts: support of a scholar by his father-in-law (kest)
